title: Loose Pieces on the Table
aka: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
story: Your little brother tipped out a box of bricks numbered 0 to n - 1 and snapped them together all afternoon, logging each snap as a pair like [2, 5].

Before tidying up, you want to know how many separate pieces are on the table. A piece is any group of bricks held together, directly or through other bricks. An untouched brick is a piece on its own.
task: Write countPieces(n, snaps). There are n bricks, numbered 0 to n - 1. Each [a, b] in snaps means bricks a and b were snapped together. Return the number of separate pieces.
The same pair can appear more than once, and snaps can close loops (like 0-1, 1-2, 2-0). Neither changes which bricks are joined.
constraints: 0 ≤ a, b < n and a ≠ b

examples.explanation: Bricks 0, 1 and 2 form one piece (0 joins 2 through 1). Bricks 4 and 5 form a second. Untouched brick 3 is a third.

The last two snaps add nothing: 2-0 closes a loop and 0-1 repeats. Bricks 0, 1, 2 are one piece and 3 another, so the answer is 2. Subtracting one piece per snap (4 bricks minus 4 snaps = 0) would be wrong, because snaps that repeat or close a loop do not join anything new.

hints: Start with every brick as its own piece: n pieces. How does the snap [0, 1] in the first example change the count? When does a snap not change it?
A snap lowers the count by one exactly when its two bricks were in different pieces. Otherwise it changes nothing.
So you need to ask "already in the same piece?" and to merge two pieces, both fast. Give every piece one brick as its leader.

Use union-find. Keep parent[i], starting as i. find(x) follows parents up to the leader. For each snap, find both leaders; if they differ, point one at the other and subtract one from the count. Shortening paths as find walks them keeps it fast.
bruteForce: For each snap, scan all n bricks and give everything in the second brick's piece the first brick's label. Count distinct labels at the end.

That is 5,000 snaps × 2,000 bricks = 10 million steps. It works, but union-find handles each snap in nearly constant time. Building an adjacency list and running a depth-first search from each unvisited brick is also fine here.

* @param {number[][]} snaps  each [a, b] joins two bricks

two halves merged later, plus a loop
pairs from the outside in, 3 untouched in the middle
loops inside each piece: n minus snaps would be 0

js: const parent = Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => i);
parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]; // shorten the path as we go
parent[ra] = rb; // merge two different pieces

parent[ra] = rb  # merge two different pieces
walkthrough: Start with n pieces. Each snap either joins two different pieces, lowering the count by one, or joins bricks already connected, changing nothing. Union-find answers "already connected?" quickly by giving each piece a leader.
Trace the second example, n = 4, snaps 0-1, 1-2, 2-0, 0-1. Start: parent = [0, 1, 2, 3], pieces = 4.
• Snap 2-0. find(2) is 2. find(0) walks 0 → 1 → 2, also 2. Same piece: skip.
Answer: 2. Brick 3 was its own leader throughout.
The line parent[x] = parent[parent[x]] makes each brick on the walk skip one level up, so over many calls the trees stay flat and find stays fast.
solution.timeWhy: m snaps, two finds each. Path shortening keeps each find at O(log n) amortized, close to constant in practice; adding union by size makes it almost exactly constant.
solution.takeaway: When connections arrive one by one and you need the number of groups, use union-find: start with n groups and subtract one each time a connection joins two different leaders.
